approach_variants.name: Bedal Creek Trail #705 (FR 4096)
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep, once the forest band below 4,900 ft is clear of snow
approach_variants.notes:
From the Mountain Loop Highway take FR 4096, a rough narrow spur where high clearance genuinely helps, to the Bedal Creek trailhead at about 2,790 ft. Distance and gain above are the full round trip by this line.

Walk the old Bedal Creek trail roughly 1.5 miles and 700 ft. It is overgrown in stretches but stays followable. The critical junction is around 3,500 ft, where a climbers' path turns off to the LEFT near 48.0560, -121.3631; it has carried pink flagging tape in recent years. Missing that turn is the standard error here — the old tread continues and dies in a brushy washout below the basin.

The climbers' path gains about 1,400 ft steeply through forest. At roughly 4,900 ft it breaks out into talus, then bends southeast through meadow and scattered timber to the Bedal-Sloan saddle at 5,300 ft, where a shallow, somewhat stagnant pond marks the usual camp. This is the last easy water; cascading streams just below the saddle are the alternative.

Southeast from the saddle the ground opens into scramble terrain. At about 5,800 ft you cross a minor rock ridge and get your first view of the glacier. Snow from here is often firm in the morning and may want axe and crampons.
approach_variants.baseFinding: The Corkscrew does not begin at the glacier — it begins after you are off it. Cross the Sloan Glacier and keep going until you are standing on bare rock at the southeast edge of the summit block, around 7,300 ft; that bare-rock arrival is where parties cache rope, axe and crampons, and it is the single most reliable confirmation on the route. From there a boot track runs along heather ledges for ten to fifteen minutes. Watch to your RIGHT for a gully of pale, near-white rock and take that. Two negatives to check yourself against: if you are still on snow or ice you have not reached the start, and if you have walked the heather for much more than a quarter hour with no white-rock gully on the right, you are contouring too low — climb.
hazards: Losing the 3,500 ft climbers'-path junction and ending in the brushy washout
Firm early-morning snow on the open slopes above 5,800 ft
Crevasses on the Sloan Glacier, normally bridged but open in lean years
Rough, narrow FR 4096 access spur

approach_variants.name: North Fork Sauk / Cougar Creek (FR 49)
approach_variants.season: Jul-Aug, after the North Fork Sauk drops from snowmelt flow
approach_variants.notes:
The start is an UNSIGNED climbers' pullout on FR 49 (Sloan Creek Road) at roughly 1,900 ft, on the north side of the North Fork Sauk. It is not the maintained North Fork Sauk River Trail #649 — that is a different trailhead a short distance back along the road, and taking it is the common mistake.

The path runs flat and brushy through stinging nettle and then devil's club for a few tenths of a mile before dropping to the river. The river must be forded or crossed on a log jam; jams are usually adequate around half a mile in but shift from year to year and are a poor bet in high water. The path then crosses river braids two or three times over the next mile before turning up Cougar Creek on a faint, intermittently cairned and flagged track through sandy streambed and forest.

Around 3,000-3,200 ft the path crosses Cougar Creek itself; lower crossings can be impassable, so hold out for the 3.2K-ish one. Steep forest switchbacks follow, passing a waterfall on Cougar Creek near 5,000 ft — roughly two to two and a half hours from the car and the last reliable water before the basin. Above the falls the track leaves the trees onto scree and slabs and angles up to the 5,800 ft basin on Sloan's northeast side, where there is a small stream and the standard bivy. This line converges with the Bedal Creek approach around 5,000-5,500 ft.
approach_variants.baseFinding: Same as the Bedal line: from the basin, ledges and slabs lead to the toe of the Sloan Glacier — rope and gear up there, not earlier. The climbing begins only once you are back on bare rock at the southeast edge of the summit block near 7,300 ft, and the entry is the gully of pale rock on your RIGHT, ten to fifteen minutes along the heather ledges from where you leave the ice.
hazards: Fording or log-crossing the North Fork Sauk — deep, cold and fast in early season
Log jams that move year to year and cannot be relied on
Devil's club and nettle on the lower path
Faint, easily lost tread up the Cougar Creek streambed

approach_variants.name: Bedal Creek Trail #705 (FR 4096)
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep, once the forest band below 4,900 ft is clear of snow
approach_variants.notes:
This row describes the same line as the Corkscrew Route; the approach is identical. FR 4096 off the Mountain Loop Highway to the Bedal Creek trailhead at about 2,790 ft, then the old Bedal Creek trail for roughly 1.5 miles and 700 ft.

At around 3,500 ft a climbers' path turns off to the LEFT near 48.0560, -121.3631, usually carrying pink flagging. It climbs about 1,400 ft steeply through forest, breaks into talus near 4,900 ft, then runs southeast through meadow to the Bedal-Sloan saddle at 5,300 ft with its shallow pond and camp — the last easy water.

Southeast from the saddle over increasingly open scramble ground; a minor rock ridge at about 5,800 ft gives the first view of the glacier.
approach_variants.baseFinding: Cross the Sloan Glacier to bare rock on the southeast edge of the summit block, roughly 7,300 ft — that is where glacier gear gets cached and where the west-face scramble actually starts. Follow the heather-ledge boot track ten to fifteen minutes and turn up the gully of pale, near-white rock on your RIGHT. Still on snow means not yet there; heather with no white gully on the right after a quarter hour means you are too low.
hazards: Losing the 3,500 ft climbers'-path junction
Firm morning snow above 5,800 ft
Crevasses on the Sloan Glacier

approach_variants.name: Bedal Creek to the West Face meadows
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
approach_variants.notes:
FR 4096 off the Mountain Loop Highway to the Bedal Creek trailhead at about 2,790 ft; Bedal Creek Trail #705 along the creek through old growth until the maintained tread gives out at a washout below the West Face basin, roughly one and a half to two and a half miles in.

Scramble the washout to a cairned exit onto the climbers' path — it leaves LEFT near 48.0560, -121.3631 around 3,500 ft and is usually flagged pink — then climb steeply through forest to about 4,900 ft, cross talus and a meadow bench, and reach the Bedal-Sloan saddle at 5,300 ft. Water here or at the streams just below.

From the saddle stay in the meadows below the broad West Face. Do not continue southeast toward the glacier toe.
approach_variants.baseFinding: The Northwest Buttress is reached on foot with no glacier travel at all, and that is the test: if you are putting crampons on, you have walked past it onto the standard Corkscrew line. From the meadows, the route starts at the lowest and left-most point of the face, on a corner of noticeably DARKER rock than the wall either side of it. Rock you can walk up to dry-shod, with grass and meadow underfoot rather than ice, is the correct base.
hazards: Brushy, blowdown-choked washout where the maintained trail ends
Route-finding through the forest band above the washout
Loose rock in the meadow-to-face transition

approach_variants.name: Bedal Creek to the Southwest Face basin
approach_variants.season: Aug-Sep, once the approach snow has cleared
approach_variants.notes:
FR 4096 off the Mountain Loop Highway to the Bedal Creek trailhead, about 2,790-2,800 ft. Bedal Creek Trail #705 through old growth along the creek's steep banks; the maintained tread peters out roughly one and a half to two and a half miles in at a large brushy washout below the basin.

Scrambling the washout is the route-finding crux of the approach. Look for a cairn marking the exit onto the climbers' path — it leaves LEFT around 3,500 ft near 48.0560, -121.3631 and is often flagged with pink tape — and follow it in steep forest switchbacks to about 4,900 ft.

Above treeline the path crosses talus and a meadow bench between 4,900 and 5,300 ft, passing a stagnant tarn at the Bedal-Sloan saddle. Last reliable water is there or at the cascading streams just below. The ground beyond turns rocky and exposed toward the glacier toe at about 5,800 ft.

A fit party familiar with the line reaches the base in around three hours. The Cougar Creek / North Fork Sauk trailhead on FR 49 converges with this line between 5,000 and 5,500 ft but adds a ford of the North Fork Sauk.
approach_variants.baseFinding: The Southwest Face and the standard Corkscrew part company at the saddle, and the discriminator is a low connecting ridge rather than a signpost. From the 5,300 ft saddle, CROSS the low ridge that divides the West Face basin from the Southwest Face basin and drop into the meadows on its far side. The Southwest Face wall rises straight out of meadow — you should reach its foot without touching snow or ice. If you find yourself roping up for glacier travel, you have followed the Corkscrew line and the face you want is behind and to your right.
hazards: Boulder- and blowdown-choked washout at the end of the maintained tread
Steep, exposed scrambling above the meadow bench
Firm snow near the glacier toe early in the season
Ford of the North Fork Sauk if using the FR 49 alternative

approach_variants.name: Bedal Creek to the Southwest Face basin
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
approach_variants.notes:
Bedal Creek is the preferred trailhead for this side of the peak because it avoids the river fords. FR 4096 off the Mountain Loop Highway, about 18.25 miles south of Darrington and roughly a mile south of Bedal Campground; the spur is rough and narrow. Trailhead about 2,790 ft.

Bedal Creek Trail #705 through old growth and along the creek's steep banks until the tread ends at a large washout, roughly one and a half to two and a half miles in. Scramble the washout to a cairned exit onto the climbers' path, which leaves LEFT near 48.0560, -121.3631 around 3,500 ft under pink flagging and switchbacks steeply up to about 4,900 ft. Talus and meadow then lead to the 5,300 ft Bedal-Sloan saddle — last reliable water before the wall.

The Cougar Creek / North Fork Sauk alternative from FR 49 reaches the same basin from the north but requires fording the North Fork Sauk plus a cold Cougar Creek crossing, slide alder and devil's club. Either way this is a full day of walking before a long rock route.
approach_variants.baseFinding: From the saddle, cross the low connecting ridge into the Southwest Face basin and its meadows rather than continuing onto the glacier. The base of the wall is gained from meadow and talus, dry-shod. Stepping onto glacier ice means you are on the Corkscrew approach, not this one.
hazards: Large washout with loose boulders and blowdown at the end of the maintained trail
Brush and real route-finding in the forest band
North Fork Sauk ford if approaching from FR 49
Long committing day — the base alone is most of a full day's walking

approach_variants.name: Barlow Pass, Gothic Basin Trail #724, Foggy Lake
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep; the trail's snow gully can need an axe into July
approach_variants.notes:
Distance and gain are round trip. Start at the Barlow Pass trailhead, about 2,360 ft, where the Mountain Loop Highway pavement ends. Walk the gated road roughly a mile to the signed junction for the Weden Creek / Gothic Basin Trail #724, which branches RIGHT off the old railroad grade.

The trail climbs steeply and steadily through timber, fording Weden Creek about a mile past the junction — a wet rock-hop in early season or after rain. Roughly 1.2 miles above the creek, and about three miles from the trailhead, the trail crosses a steep avalanche gully that runs as a cascading waterfall in summer but can hold a firm, consequential snow tongue well into July. That crossing is the main hazard on the walk in.

Above treeline the trail breaks into the meadows and rock slabs of Gothic Basin around 5,000 ft. The meadows are fragile — travel on rock and gravel where possible. From the basin a boot path runs past a small tarn and up boulder and talus slopes to Foggy Lake at about 5,200 ft, roughly 3.3 miles in. The lake is the last reliable water and the last flat staging or camping ground.

From Foggy Lake, cross the boulder field on the climbers' trail along the lake's north side, then work up Del Campo's south-facing slopes toward the permanent snowfield below the summit walls at roughly 6,200 ft.
approach_variants.baseFinding: At the top of the snowfield you face a rock wall with one obvious gully splitting it. THE OBVIOUS GULLY IS THE WRONG LINE: it looks like the natural way, and it steepens and ends against a vertical wall about a hundred vertical feet below the top. The correct start is the blocky, staircase-like class 3-4 ledge system immediately to climber's LEFT of that gully. It carries a boot path — if there is a bootpath under your feet you are on it, if you are on clean untracked rock in a narrowing groove you are not. The ledges lead to a notch on the southeast ridge at about 6,350 ft; from the notch turn LEFT (west) for the last short scramble to the true summit at 6,610 ft. If the ground you are on constricts into a chimney and turns class 4 near its top, you are in the gully — reverse and move left onto the ledges. Parties who scramble directly to the notch on 4th class have simply missed the class 3 ledges a little further left.
hazards: Steep snow tongue where the trail crosses the avalanche gully, into July
Weden Creek ford
Loose rock on the upper wall — helmet from Foggy Lake onward
Blind entry into the dead-end gully in cloud

approach_variants.name: Barlow Pass, Gothic Basin Trail #724, Foggy Lake outlet
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep; cairns can be buried by snow into early summer
approach_variants.notes:
Distance is round trip to Foggy Lake. Start at the Barlow Pass trailhead on the Mountain Loop Highway, about 19.3 miles east of the Verlot Public Service Center, on the Weden Creek / Gothic Basin trail (USFS #724).

The first two thirds of a mile follows an old closed mining road before singletrack begins climbing through forest. The trail fords Weden Creek at around 1.1 miles — no bridge, and the main reliable water low on the route. Above that it switchbacks up a steep root-and-rock staircase, gaining close to 1,000 ft per mile through a roughly two-mile band that is the physical crux of the walk. That section holds lingering snow patches and old avalanche debris across the tread well into early summer in heavy years.

At about 3.5 to 4 miles the trail breaks out of timber into the open slabs and tarns of Gothic Basin — the last dependable water and a sensible bail-out point in bad weather. Continue up talus and slab benches another half mile and roughly 600 ft to the saddle above Foggy Lake, then drop slightly and traverse three or four tenths of a mile along and above the shore to the lake's OUTLET.
approach_variants.baseFinding: The scramble begins at the lake's OUTLET, not from a random point on the shore, and getting on it early or late is the usual error. From the outlet, look up at the obvious low point on Gothic's southeast ridge. The line is NOT the ridge crest: stay in the SCREE on the climber's RIGHT of the crest and follow the cairns, which are numerous and continuous, past a small tarn at the foot of a snowfield. Cairns underfoot and scree, not rock, is the confirmation. At the very top, where the summit block stops the scree, cut LEFT onto a narrow sidewalk of downsloping rock — slightly exposed easy friction — and switchback back up and right to the base of the block; the final scramble is about 30 ft of low-exposure class 3. Two negatives: if you are on the crest itself you have drifted right off the easy line, and if you find yourself on exposed class 4 to climber's LEFT just below the summit block you have gone too far left, which is where most parties who get into trouble end up. In early season the cairns can be buried and the correct line is genuinely hard to hold.
hazards: Snow patches and avalanche debris across the tread in the steep timber band
Weden Creek ford
Buried cairns in early season, leading parties onto exposed class 4 left of the correct line

approach_variants.name: Sunrise Mine Trail #707, Headlee Pass, Vesper-Wolf saddle
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep; the ledge traverse holds snow into mid-summer
approach_variants.notes:
Sunrise Mine Road (FR 4065) leaves the Mountain Loop Highway roughly 27-28 miles east of Granite Falls; about 2.3-2.5 miles of gravel end at the Sunrise Mine trailhead, around 2,400 ft, with a pit toilet and a Northwest Forest Pass requirement.

Trail #707 starts in second-growth and almost immediately crosses the South Fork Stillaguamish on logs — a genuine obstacle in high runoff. It then climbs through Wirtz Basin and out onto open cairned talus to Headlee Pass, about 4,720 ft at 2.7 miles: a narrow rocky notch with loose footing where rockfall from parties above is a real hazard. Beyond the pass the trail drops through trees and crosses about a third of a mile of talus to Vesper Creek, following it up to Vesper Lake (Lake Elan) at about 4,950 ft and 3.5 miles. That is the last dependable running water.

The north-face routes are NOT approached from the lake basin. Stay on the ordinary Vesper summit trail up talus and slabs to roughly 5,600-5,700 ft, then leave it and swing NORTH across the slabs. Allow three hours or more from the car to the base.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The confirmation that you are in the right place to start traversing is TWO LARGE CAIRNS on a saddle at about 5,700 ft, near 48.01375 -121.51451, with Copper Lake visible below to the northwest. Do not drop into the saddle. The heather-covered ledge system starts about 30 ft ABOVE the cairns on third-class slabs and runs east across the north face for roughly 800 ft, with a goat trail worn through it; there is one exposed step down off the saddle before it widens.

Sources name this saddle inconsistently — the mapped approach calls it the Vesper-Wolf saddle, several route write-ups call it the Vesper-Sperry col. The two cairns and the view of Copper Lake are the reliable test, not the name.

At the far end of the traverse, where the ledge runs out, the ORIGINAL start goes up and then right on about 60 ft of low fifth to third-class slabs and an obvious flaky gully. The cleaner and now more common variation is reached by backtracking slightly and making an exposed third-class traverse down and around the toe of a buttress to a clean 5.6 LAYBACK FLAKE. Negative marker: Ragged Edge jogs hard RIGHT within the first pitch or two. A first pitch that runs straight up the face and stays there is True Grit, not this route.
hazards: Rockfall from parties above in the Headlee Pass couloir
Log crossing of the South Fork Stillaguamish in high runoff
Steep exposed heather on the ledge traverse — treacherous when wet
Snow on the ledge traverse into mid-to-late summer; axe worth carrying early season

approach_variants.name: Sunrise Mine Trail #707, Headlee Pass, Vesper-Wolf saddle
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep; expect steep snow on the ledge traverse in June
approach_variants.notes:
From Granite Falls drive the Mountain Loop Highway about 27-28 miles, turn onto Sunrise Mine Road (FR 4065) and follow roughly 2.3-2.5 miles of gravel to the Sunrise Mine trailhead at about 2,400 ft. Northwest Forest Pass; pit toilet on site.

Sunrise Mine Trail #707 runs about 2.7-3 miles and 2,600 ft to Headlee Pass at 4,720 ft, crossing the South Fork Stillaguamish on logs low down and passing through Wirtz Basin onto cairned talus. Past the pass the trail continues around Sperry Peak's south flank into the Vesper Creek and lake basin, then the main summit trail climbs talus and slabs to about 5,600-5,700 ft. Leave the trail there and head north/northwest across the slabs.
approach_variants.baseFinding: Two large cairns mark the saddle at roughly 5,700 ft, near 48.01375 -121.51451, with Copper Lake in view to the northwest — that is the marker, and it is what you look for in cloud. Third-class slabs about 30 ft ABOVE the cairns lead onto the heather-covered ledges of the north face. Traverse those ledges roughly 800 ft eastward to reach the original start near 48.01376 -121.51736, gained by fourth-class moves on an up-then-right arch. An alternative start uses a small notch overlooking the remnant Vesper Glacier. If you have dropped into the saddle rather than climbing 30 ft above it, you are below the ledge system and it will not go.
hazards: Rockfall in the Headlee Pass couloir
Steep snow on the ledge traverse in June — ice axe and crampons
Wet heather on the traverse
Log crossing of the South Fork Stillaguamish

approach_variants.name: Sunrise Mine Trail #707, Headlee Pass, Vesper-Wolf saddle
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep; earlier needs axe and crampons for the ledge traverse
approach_variants.notes:
Sunrise Mine trailhead off the Mountain Loop Highway via Sunrise Mine Road (FR 4065). Trail #707 crosses the South Fork Stillaguamish on a log almost immediately — a real obstacle in high runoff — then climbs through Wirtz Basin, breaks into cairned talus and boulder fields, and reaches Headlee Pass at about 4,720 ft and 2.7 miles. The pass is a narrow rocky notch with loose footing where rockfall from above is a genuine hazard.

Past the pass the trail drops briefly through trees, crosses about a third of a mile of talus to Vesper Creek and follows it up to Vesper Lake (Lake Elan) at about 4,950 ft, 3.5 miles and 2,700 ft from the car — last reliable water.

Stay on the ordinary Vesper summit trail up talus and slabs to roughly 5,600-5,700 ft, then leave it and swing north across the slabs. Three hours or more car to base.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Aim for the two large cairns on the saddle at about 5,700 ft (near 48.01375 -121.51451), with Copper Lake below to the northwest; the heather ledge system starts about 30 ft ABOVE the cairns on third-class slabs, not from the saddle floor. Traverse east on the goat trail through the heather.

True Grit itself is identified by its first anchor, not by its first moves. Pitch 1 is about 200 ft of easy, clean granite and finishes by stepping LEFT to a BOLTED belay sitting directly beneath an obvious NARROW CHIMNEY. If there is no chimney above the anchor you have reached, you are not on True Grit. It is the more direct of the two lines here — Ragged Edge jogs sharply right in its first pitch or two, so a line that keeps going straight up is this one.
hazards: Rockfall in the Headlee Pass couloir
Steep exposed heather benches, slick when wet
Snow on the ledge traverse into early-to-mid summer
Loose rock on the face — treat as alpine despite the bolted belays

approach_variants.name: Sunrise Mine Trail #707, Headlee Pass, Vesper-Wolf saddle
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep; the ledge traverse holds snow into mid-summer
approach_variants.notes:
Identical to True Grit and Ragged Edge. Sunrise Mine Trail #707 from the Sunrise Mine trailhead: log crossing of the South Fork Stillaguamish, Wirtz Basin, cairned talus, Headlee Pass at about 4,720 ft and 2.7 miles with loose rock and rockfall exposure in the narrow couloir, then down to Vesper Creek and Vesper Lake (Lake Elan) at about 4,950 ft and 3.5 miles — last water.

Stay on the summit trail to roughly 5,600-5,700 ft, leave it and swing north across the slabs to the saddle with the two large cairns at about 5,700 ft. The heather ledges start about 30 ft above the cairns; traverse east on the goat trail across the north face. Plan three hours or more to the base.
approach_variants.baseFinding: Fish & Whistle is not a separate landmark on the traverse — it is found by reference to True Grit. Continue the same ledge traverse and the start is at a LARGE TREE about 50 ft LEFT (west) of True Grit's start, on the talus and boulder apron directly under the north face. The confirmation is the first pitch itself: a clean friction slab passing FIVE BOLTS in about 80 ft. Neither True Grit nor Ragged Edge begins on a bolt ladder up open slab, so five bolts in a row is the check. If you have walked past the tree and are on ground with no bolted slab above it, you have gone too far along the ledges.
hazards: Rockfall in the Headlee Pass couloir
Slick, exposed heather on the ledge traverse
Snow lingering on the traverse into mid-to-late summer
Runout friction climbing off the deck on pitch 1

approach_variants.name: South Fork log crossing to Dry Creek basin
approach_variants.season: Late spring to summer — after the couloir snow consolidates, before it melts to bare loose rock
approach_variants.notes:
Two starts reach the same ground: the Big Four Picnic Area / Ice Caves trailhead at about 1,640 ft, or the Mount Dickerman trailhead across the highway, which lands you nearer the drainage. Either way, walk to the South Fork Stillaguamish and hunt up and down the bank for a large sound log — there is no bridge, but several substantial logs are usually available.

On the south bank travel southeasterly through open forest, roughly a mile, with heavy log debris and tall vegetation obstructing the line. A dense band of slide alder guards the forest edge before the creek; turning west generally avoids most of it.

Follow the broad, smoother bed of Dry Creek upward. Water surfaces around 2,200 ft. The headwall ahead carries a visible waterfall. Above the headwall, the upper basin opens onto talus.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
There is more than one gully in the headwall and the choice matters. The NORTHERNMOST gully is the winter line. In dry conditions take the one trending WEST toward the upper basin, gained by a series of class 3-4 ledges and ramps rather than by a snow chute; in snow conditions the hidden chute goes instead.

From the upper basin, walk SOUTH across several gullies before you commit. The correct main couloir is the one that is noticeably NARROWER than the ones you crossed to get there, and it is the point where crampons go on. A gully you can stroll into without committing is not it — the right one is steep and offers no reprieve from the first steps. Higher, a steep gully or snowfinger leads to a small cave, from where a rightward class 4 traverse on RED slabby rock gains the South Ridge of the Main Peak; red rock underfoot on that traverse is the confirmation.
hazards: Unbridged log crossing of the South Fork Stillaguamish
Dense slide alder at the forest edge below Dry Creek
Steep, icy, committing main couloir with no escape once started
Exposed class 4 on the red slabs
Heavy blowdown and pathless forest travel — no trail of any kind

approach_variants.name: Ice Caves nature trail to the north face basin
approach_variants.season: Winter to early spring — deliberately an early-season line
approach_variants.notes:
The shortest approach on this list. Walk the nearly wheelchair-accessible paved nature trail from the Big Four Picnic Area toward the ice caves, and continue to the open basin below the north face. The face rises about 4,000 ft directly above.

From the trail's end move RIGHT to find the break in the lower cliff band. With adequate snow cover this is straightforward walking; in a sparse-snow year the only way through is a bushwhack far out to the right.
approach_variants.baseFinding: The lower cliff band is the gate, and whether it is open is the first thing to read. With the face in condition the break on the right goes as a snow walk and deposits you in the basin under the couloir; if you are forced into bushwhacking out on the far right to get through, the face is thin and the route is out of nick. The route was established in early March after a week of rain followed by a cold snap, which is the pattern that brings it in.
hazards: Spindrift avalanches down the couloir — the route is named for them
Avalanche hazard on the whole north face in winter
Thin cliff-band break in low-snow years forcing exposed bushwhacking
No retreat once committed to the couloir

approach_variants.name: Lake Serene Trail #1068 to the north side of North Peak
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep, after several consecutive dry days
approach_variants.notes:
From US-2 at milepost 35.2 turn south on Mount Index Road and drive 0.3 miles to the Lake Serene trailhead at about 600 ft. Lake Serene Trail #1068 runs roughly 3.6 to 4.1 miles and about 2,000 ft to the lake at around 2,600 ft, passing the Bridal Veil Falls spur near mile 1.6. The maintained trail ends at the lake's north end.

From there, traverse talus and very large boulders along the west and south side of the lake, near an old rockslide, toward the base of North Peak's wall. In early season this crossing goes over avalanche debris and snow and ice piled at the water's edge.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The climbing does not start on the clean wall you first walk under. The original line begins on the broken, BUSHY SPUR on the northeast, which rises out of the wooded ridge above the lake — you start on third and fourth class slabs and grass, not on clean rock. The confirmation is uncomfortable but reliable: the first few hundred feet are downsloping holds on generally solid slab, often sopping wet with moss, and that is what being on route feels like here. Dry, clean, positive rock at the start means you have wandered onto one of the harder faces.

The first fixed reference above the slabs is a VERTICAL WALL with a TWO-PITON ANCHOR — that is the normal point to rope up. Above it a ramp system passes as the 'hidden ledge', then a steep brush tunnel with vertical ten- to twenty-foot steps pulled on vegetation. Between roughly 3,000 and 3,600 ft the brush is at its worst. This face does not dry out at the rate other alpine rock does; several dry days beforehand are part of the route conditions, not a nicety.
hazards: Wet moss on downsloping slabs — low-angle ground that is genuinely serious
Avalanche debris and lingering snow at the lake edge in early season
Vertical brush steps with no protection
Loose, vegetated rock throughout; slow retreat

approach_variants.name: Lake Serene Trail #1068 to the North Peak north face
approach_variants.season: Jul-Aug for dry rock across all three summits
approach_variants.notes:
US-2 at milepost 35.2, south on Mount Index Road 0.3 miles to the Lake Serene trailhead at about 600 ft. Lake Serene Trail #1068 runs about 4 miles and 2,000 ft to the lake basin; the maintained trail ends at the lake's north end.

Traverse the WEST side of the lake over talus and very large boulders to its south end, then climb steep brush and a gully system toward the base of North Peak's north face. That gully carries snow into early summer.

Budget headlamps in the morning to reach the lake so the technical section starts at first light: parties commonly need 12 to 15 hours or more, and many bivy.
approach_variants.baseFinding: The traverse begins by climbing the North Face route on North Peak, and its start is a broken, bushy spur rather than a clean wall — third and fourth class slabs and grass, frequently wet, with downsloping holds. That wetness and vegetation is the confirmation, not a sign you are off route. A vertical wall with a two-piton anchor above the initial slabs is the normal rope-up point. Between about 3,000 and 3,600 ft the brush is thickest; it forms a tunnel with vertical ten- to twenty-foot steps. Clean, dry, steep rock at the start means you have drifted onto a harder line.
hazards: Wet mossy slabs on the lower face
Steep brush with vertical steps and no protection
Rotten rock and sparse protection on the ridge between summits
Notches on the traverse needing careful downclimbing or short rappels
Very long committing day with poor escape options

approach_variants.name: Lake Serene Trail #1068 to the North Peak north face
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep — enough snow gone from the ledges to protect the rock, before on-route water dries up
approach_variants.notes:
Lake Serene trailhead at about 600 ft off Mount Index Road. The maintained, well-graded Lake Serene Trail runs roughly 4.1 miles and about 2,000 ft, passing the Bridal Veil Falls viewpoint spur near mile 1.6, to Lake Serene at about 2,600 ft.

At the lake, leave the maintained trail for the unofficial climbers' path across talus and large boulders along the west and south shore toward the base of North Index's face. Early season this crosses avalanche debris and snow piled at the lake's edge.
approach_variants.baseFinding: The route climbs directly up a brushy TUNNEL on North Peak's lower face, and the entry is recognised by texture rather than by shape: steepening mossy slabs and third/fourth class rock that is often wet and downsloping — treat it as low fifth in practice — leading into thick brush with several vertical ten- to twenty-foot steps of shrub-pulling. That is the correct ground. This face section alone routinely takes many hours; parties have reported barely reaching halfway after ten hours of climbing, so slow progress is not evidence you are off route. From North Peak's summit the line continues as an exposed ridge over the top of the Norwegian Buttresses to Middle Peak and on to Main Peak, with notches requiring downclimbing or short rappels.
hazards: Wet mossy downsloping slabs low on the face
Vertical brush steps with no protection
Avalanche debris at the lake in early season
Committing ridge with limited escape once past North Peak

approach_variants.name: Lake Serene Trail #1068, south-end saddle, southwest ridge
approach_variants.season: Snow cover — roughly late winter through May; not recommended once melted out
approach_variants.notes:
Lake Serene trailhead off Mount Index Road at about 600 ft. Lake Serene Trail #1068 runs about 4.1 miles and 2,000 ft to the north end of the lake, where the trail ends.

Traverse the WEST side of the lake over talus and huge boulders to the south end. In snow, stay lower, closer to the water — the slope is less steep near the shore. Expect massive avalanche debris on this stretch.

From the south end of the lake head EAST to the saddle, then take the ridge running SOUTHWEST from it. That forested ridge is the crux of the approach and the reason this is a spring route: roughly the next 1,000 ft is dense brush and intermittent cliffs, plus one airy ten-foot rock step usually climbed by grabbing roots. Snow cover makes the ridge dramatically easier; bare, it is a fight. Plan on 12+ hours car to car and over 6,000 ft of gain despite the peak being under 6,000 ft.
approach_variants.baseFinding: Follow the ridge until it runs into the cliffs of Index, then TRAVERSE UNDER the cliffs and take the FIRST WIDE gully on your RIGHT. That is the Hourglass. Its shape is the check: it is wide and easy where you enter, constricts high up, then opens again. A gully that is narrow at the point where you step into it is not the one — keep traversing. Once melted out, the constriction holds a large wet rock step; that step is the reason the route is climbed as a snow line rather than in summer, and passing it dry would be mid-to-high fifth on the right side via a short chimney and face, or harder on the left.
hazards: Steep dense brush and intermittent cliffs on the forested southwest ridge
The airy ten-foot rock step on the ridge, usually climbed on roots
Avalanche debris and avalanche hazard around the lake and in the gully
The wet rock step in the constriction once the gully melts out
Very long day — 12 to 15 hours is normal

approach_variants.name: Climbers' path behind the Barclay Lake trailhead outhouse
approach_variants.season: May-Oct; the notch gully holds snow into mid-summer
approach_variants.notes:
Distance and gain are round trip to the true summit. Drive US-2 to milepost 42 in Baring — the turnoff is directly across from the store — and turn north onto Barclay Creek Road (FR 6024). Cross the railroad tracks immediately and bear LEFT at the fork about 0.2 miles up. Roughly 4.3 to 4.5 miles of gravel reach the Barclay Lake trailhead at about 2,280 ft: parking for around 20 cars, a vault toilet, picnic tables, and no potable water.

Do NOT start on Barclay Creek Trail 1055. The climbers' path begins BEHIND THE OUTHOUSE, on the overgrown abandoned logging road that continues uphill from the parking area. Follow that road two or three tenths of a mile to the first creek. Look RIGHT for a cairn where a steep, heavily eroded path turns straight uphill toward the ridge. Orange, green or pink tape has been reported and may or may not be present.

You cross the creek twice — that double crossing is a useful confirmation you are on the correct path. From there the path climbs relentlessly and directly up the forested north/west side, with a short badly eroded class 3 step where hand lines have been reported, and several places where the tread braids. Trekking poles help on the loose lower section. There is no reliable water above the creek.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The transition from approach to route is a change in the ground, not a landmark: the path tops out on the WEST RIDGE CREST at about 4,000-4,100 ft, where the angle suddenly eases and the tread visibly improves. If you are still fighting steep eroded dirt, you have not reached it.

Follow the crest east for roughly a mile. Where the cliff bands appear you must drop BELOW them — this is where parties go wrong. Staying high on the crest feels natural and cliffs you out, forcing steep and dangerous downclimbing to recover; hold a lower trajectory, cross the wooded gully, pick up the faint path on the far side and traverse into the talus basin at about 4,900 ft. From the basin the main gully to the notch at about 5,550 ft between South Baring and the true summit is obvious and navigation is straightforward. A 2022 burn scar on the south-facing slope has left loose ash and dirt that can obscure the tread along the crest.
hazards: Very steep, loose, heavily eroded lower path — braided tread easy to lose
Cliffing out by staying high on the west ridge crest
Loose ash and obscured tread through the 2022 burn scar
Snow in the notch gully into mid-summer; the step at the notch varies year to year with snowpack
Loose rock in the summit basin — helmet
Creek crossings have been a ford when the log is out

approach_variants.name: Climbers' path behind the Barclay Lake trailhead outhouse
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep; the basin and notch gully hold snow late
approach_variants.notes:
Note that this row and the Northwest Ridge row describe the same physical climbers' path up the west side of the mountain; the naming differs by source, the ground does not.

Barclay Lake trailhead at about 2,200-2,280 ft at the end of FR 6024 / Barclay Creek Road, shared parking with the Barclay Lake day hike. Go around the outhouse and pick up the old overgrown logging-road grade for a few hundred yards before it turns sharply uphill into a steep, muddy, eroded gully — that is the start of the unmaintained climbers' trail. Look for cairns and boot tread; this is not a maintained trail and is easy to lose. The tread is steep and often slick from the first steps, and there is no reliable water past the initial creek, so fill up at the car.

After roughly a mile and 1,800 ft the path tops out on Baring's west ridge at about 4,000 ft.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The west ridge crest at about 4,000 ft is the handover point — the angle eases and the tread improves noticeably. Follow the crest generally east/southeast. Where the cliff bands appear, watch for the point where the path dips slightly BELOW them into a wooded gully before regaining the ridge; staying too long on the crest is the recorded error and forces a downclimb back to the correct line. The 2022 burn scar on the south-facing slope adds loose ash and hides the tread here.

The route then drops into a talus and boulder basin, crosses it, and climbs the main gully up to the notch at about 5,550 ft between South Baring and the true summit. That gully and basin hold snow late; the step right at the notch is sometimes called the vertical snow wall and its difficulty varies year to year. From the notch scramble up and right a short way, break onto an open slope, then trend left/north over class 2-3 boulder and heather to the base of the summit block, which is climbed on its LEFT (west) side at class 3-4 to reach 6,127 ft.
hazards: Steep, muddy, eroded unmaintained tread from the first steps
Cliffing out by holding the crest too long
Loose ash and obscured tread in the burn scar
Late snow in the basin and notch gully — axe and possibly crampons into mid-summer
Loose rock from the boulder field onward — helmet
No water above the trailhead creek

approach_variants.name: Barclay Lake trailhead to Couloir Camp and the North Face
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep; snow lingers in the couloir into August
approach_variants.notes:
Barclay Lake trailhead at about 2,280 ft at the end of FR 6024 / Barclay Creek Road off US-2 near Baring; Northwest Forest Pass at the self-issue kiosk.

Leave the signed Barclay Lake trail immediately — the climbers' boot path starts BEHIND THE OUTHOUSE, not on the main trail. Follow the old abandoned logging road about a third of a mile to a cairn at roughly 2,450 ft where a rough unmaintained path splits off toward the base of the mountain. That split is easy to miss and carries no trail sign.

From the cairn the boot path climbs steep loose dirt and crosses the creek draining the face several times. STAY CLOSE TO THE WATER: the tread is faint and repeatedly lost in the brush, and the creek is the handrail. In total the lower approach fights through roughly 2,300 vertical feet of dense slide alder, vine maple and devil's club before any technical rock. Allow around seven hours from the trailhead to the base of the wall, and wear boots or sturdy approach shoes rather than carrying them.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
COULOIR CAMP at about 4,300 ft — around 2,000 ft of gain and 1.4 miles from the car — is the landmark that tells you which approach you are on. It is a used bivy shelf directly beneath the wall, historically the base camp for the first-ascent siege, and it remains a reasonable first night for parties splitting the approach. Above it, the ground to follow runs BETWEEN TWO precipitous brush-and-cliff-covered rock RIBS that flank a large couloir; snow often lingers there into August, so an axe is worth having early season. Follow that ground to the base of the North Face's first rock step at roughly 5,500 ft, about 1.8 miles from the trailhead.

Negative marker: if you have gained a ridge crest and the walking has suddenly got easier, you are on the northwest-ridge scramble line on the west side of the mountain, not on the face — the face approach never eases.
hazards: Missing the unsigned cairn split at ~2,450 ft
About 2,300 ft of slide alder, vine maple and devil's club
Faint tread constantly lost in brush — losing the creek loses the line
Steep loose dirt slopes
Snow in the couloir between the ribs into August

approach_variants.name: Barclay Creek Trail 1055 to the lake, then straight up the north face hillside
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
approach_variants.notes:
From US-2 at milepost 42 in Baring, directly across from the store, turn north onto Barclay Creek Road (FR 6024), cross the BNSF tracks and bear left at the fork about 0.2 miles up. Follow about 4.3 to 4.5 miles of gravel to the Barclay Lake trailhead at roughly 2,280 ft — parking for about 20 cars, a vault toilet, picnic tables, no potable water.

Unlike the ridge and face routes, this one uses the maintained trail: Barclay Creek Trail 1055 runs gently east up the valley about 2.2 miles to Barclay Lake at around 2,420 ft, directly beneath the wall. The north face rises roughly 3,700 vertical feet from the lake in only half a mile of horizontal distance.

Leave the trail near the lake and climb the steep forested, brushy hillside beneath the wall. The 1961 first-ascent account of this face describes the first 1,000 ft as exactly that — a brush-and-forest struggle to reach a camp below the couloirs — and nothing about that terrain has improved. Allow several hours from the car to the base.
approach_variants.baseFinding: There is NO maintained climbers' path to the main-peak wall, and that absence is itself the navigation aid. The fixed lines, hand lines and boot track that exist on this mountain belong to the DOLOMITE TOWER approach, which leaves the trail well BEFORE the lake and goes up a different drainage. If you find fixed rope, bolted slab or a worn boot track on your way to the base, you are in the wrong drainage entirely — turn around and go back to the lake. The correct ground is pathless: wet vegetation, blowdown and loose forest floor, gained by leaving the trail at the lake and going straight up.
hazards: Pathless steep brush and blowdown for the first 1,000 ft
Wet vegetation and loose ground
No fixed protection or path — retreat is by the same brush
Easy to end up on the Dolomite Tower approach in the wrong drainage

approach_variants.name: Barclay Creek Trail, right before the bridge, fixed lines to the tower
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Barclay Lake trailhead (74920 NE Stevens Pass Hwy, Skykomish). Walk the pleasant, level main Barclay Creek trail for about 20 minutes and roughly a mile to a bridge crossing a large creek — often dry by mid-to-late summer.

DO NOT CROSS THE BRIDGE. Just before it, break RIGHT into the forest around a LARGE BOULDER. Bushwhack through relatively open forest, or walk the creek bed, until you reach an open boulder field. Cross the boulder field to large trees and an open wash.

The wash leads to a steep, chossy, dirty waterfall; climb around its RIGHT side, staying out of the bushes — this stretch is exposed. Above that a ramp with hand lines, then a 60-70 degree forested rib with fixed lines and natural protection, including a low-fifth step in a gully protected by a fixed line, and a small rock face with a bolt. Then roughly 800 ft of mostly roped slab in 35-50 m pitches on bolts and natural gear. Competent parties with good beta take two and a half to four hours; the approach is technical and hard to get right even with information.
approach_variants.baseFinding: The end of the fixed and roped section is where you unrope and scramble UP AND LEFT to the base of the tower. The test the first-ascent party wrote down is a negative one and it is the most useful thing on this approach: IF WHAT YOU ARE DOING FEELS SKETCHY, YOU ARE OFF THE LINE. The approach is unpleasant but it is protected the whole way — fixed lines, hand lines, bolts — so unprotected, committing ground means you have lost the route, not that the route has got harder. The base of the tower is the foot of a nearly 1,500 ft overhanging prow; there is no mistaking it once you are under it.
hazards: Exposed scrambling around the right side of the chossy waterfall
Fixed lines of unknown age and condition
60-70 degree forested rib — a fall here is not survivable ground
Loose rock and brush throughout
Route-finding: the correct line is not obvious even with beta

approach_variants.name: Barclay Creek Trail, right before the bridge, fixed lines to the tower
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
approach_variants.notes:
Identical to Vanishing Point. Barclay Lake trailhead; walk the level main Barclay Creek trail about 20 minutes and a mile to the bridge over a large creek (often dry mid-to-late summer). Do NOT cross it — break RIGHT into forest around a large boulder just before it.

Bushwhack through open forest or up the creek bed to an open boulder field, cross it to large trees and an open wash, then climb around the RIGHT side of a steep chossy waterfall (exposed). Above, a ramp with hand lines, a 60-70 degree forested rib with fixed lines, and about 800 ft of mostly roped slab on bolts and natural features.
approach_variants.baseFinding: Reach the base of the tower as for Vanishing Point — unrope at the top of the roped slabs and scramble up and LEFT. If the ground is unprotected and feels sketchy, you have come off the approach line; the whole approach is protected. Deep Blue's first pitch starts about 100 ft LEFT of Vanishing Point's, so find Vanishing Point's start first and traverse from it rather than trying to identify Deep Blue in isolation.
hazards: Exposed scrambling around the waterfall
Fixed lines of unknown age
Steep forested rib
Loose rock and brush

approach_variants.name: FR 5620 pulloff to the base of the west peak slab
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
approach_variants.notes:
I-90 Exit 34 east of North Bend, east on Edgewick Road, then right at the stop sign after 0.4 miles onto SE Middle Fork Road, which becomes FR 56. Drive about 12.3 miles to the Middle Fork / Taylor River junction just after the Taylor River bridge, turn right onto road 5620 and go about a mile to a small gravel pulloff — five cars at most — near 47.54604, -121.52151 at about 1,174 ft. Washouts on the Middle Fork road have periodically added a mile or more of walking.

The path leaves the road a hundred to two hundred yards further along, on the left, marked by a cairn. From there it climbs steeply through forest switchbacks for roughly 30 to 45 minutes. The tread is not signed but it is genuinely worn: if you have been walking more than a few minutes on ground that does not look like a trail, you are off it.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
About 50 yards below the start of the climbing there is a LARGE CAIRN BUILT OF FLAT WHITE ROCKS — by a clear margin the biggest cairn on the approach trail, and the marker to look for. The base itself sits near 47.549, -121.5137 at about 1,700 ft.

From there the confirmation is bolts. This is a continuous bolted line up the slab, so a slab with no bolts on it is not the route. Two supporting details: the lower pitches are easy, low-angle and somewhat runout on solid, sometimes water-polished slab; and several hangers down there are visibly BENT from rockfall coming down the route, which both identifies the ground and tells you why to keep moving through it. Parties simulclimbing the easy lower pitches have gone off-track precisely by not tracking the bolts.
hazards: Rockfall down the lower slab pitches — bent hangers record it
Steep, loose, unsigned approach tread
Road washouts on the Middle Fork road adding approach distance
No water on the approach or the route

approach_variants.name: Gravel wash pullout on FR 56, dry creekbed and dirt gully
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep, and only in bone-dry conditions
approach_variants.notes:
Distance is one-way horizontal; almost all of the effort is vertical. From I-90 Exit 34 at North Bend, drive Middle Fork Snoqualmie River Road (FR 56) east — paved, then good gravel — staying on FR 56 PAST the Taylor River Road (FR 5620) junction, about 2.6 miles further, to a wide gravel wash and old borrow-pit pullout on the north side of the road at roughly 1,150-1,200 ft.

There is no maintained or numbered Forest Service trail here. This is an unmaintained climbers' boot path with intermittent cairns and pink flagging.

From the wash, follow the dry creekbed uphill for roughly a mile. A boot path exits climber's LEFT into second-growth forest with light brush before the creek narrows. Several boot-path branches exist low down: AVOID the flat, early traverse that cuts across to the slab too low, and take the higher up-and-down traverse instead.

At about 2,200 ft the path enters a loose dirt-and-scree gully mixed with vegetation — unpleasant, roughly 400 ft of gain — then exits climber's LEFT onto a wooded ridge for another 400 ft of steep but relatively brush-free ground. There is no reliable water past the creek near the trailhead.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base of the climbing is the FIRST MAJOR SLAB at about 2,900 ft, roughly an hour and 1,700 ft above the car. It is unmistakable by contrast: it is the first clean rock of the day after nothing but duff, dirt and scree. Two low-fifth pitches follow intersecting DIKES up it; parties either solo them or rope up.

The negative marker is the dirt gully. If you have arrived at slab WITHOUT first grovelling through the loose dirt-and-scree gully at about 2,200 ft, you took the low flat traverse and you are on the slab too far along — traverse up and left to regain the line. Above the slab the landmarks come in a fixed order and that order is how you confirm you are still on it: dirt and heather above the slab's upper-LEFT edge, a tiny notch, a knife-edge razorback, and then a flat bivy clearing known as the glade saddle. A short wooded ramp with one sporty 20 ft scramble step follows, then a rope-up point at an exposed ledge traverse leading to the Y Notch, where the line joins the gully locally called #2 Gully — loose rock on one side, polished mossy rock on the other — for the last 600 ft or so to the summit ridge at 5,519 ft.
hazards: No water above the trailhead creek
About 40-degree loose duff above the slab; huckleberry stems are the handholds
Slabs and dirt gullies become treacherous when even slightly wet
Braided boot paths low down leading to the slab at the wrong height
Loose and mossy rock in #2 Gully
Serious route-finding above the slab — intermittent path, cairns and flagging only

approach_variants.name: Gravel wash pullout on FR 56, dry creekbed and dirt gully
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep, bone dry only
approach_variants.notes:
I-90 Exit 34 near North Bend, then Middle Fork Snoqualmie Road (FR 56) past the Taylor River bridge junction to a pullout roughly 2.6 miles further on, beside a gravel wash. From the car the whole route is only about 1.5 miles horizontally but 4,400 vertical feet.

Start up the dry creek bed and leave it partway up into the woods, following a mix of pink flagging tape and faint tread up steep pine-needle slopes — 'scrumbling', pulling on whatever vegetation is at hand. Low down the path braids: take the higher up-and-down traverse rather than the flat early one that cuts to the slab too low. About an hour in, at roughly 2,200 ft, you reach the dirt gully.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The dirt gully at about 2,200 ft is the gate, and the first major SLAB at about 2,900 ft is the base. Clean rock after an hour of nothing but duff and scree is the confirmation. Reaching slab without having passed through the dirt gully means you took the low traverse and are too far along the base — go up and left.

Above the slab the pine-needle slopes run about 40 degrees on loose duff, and huckleberry stems make the best handholds. The sequence above is the tiny notch, the razorback, the glade saddle, the wooded ramp with a 20 ft step, the exposed ledge traverse, and then the Y Notch where the route joins the gully system. Reaching the Y is what confirms you are on the South Route rather than on one of the neighbouring gully lines.
hazards: Loose 40-degree duff above the slab
No water above the trailhead creek
Slabs lethal when damp
Braided boot path low down
Exposed ledge traverse below the Y Notch

approach_variants.name: SR-20 pullout, Burgundy Creek climbers' trail, the Bench, Burgundy Col
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the broad pullout and overlook on SR-20 near milepost 165-166, about four miles east of Washington Pass, where a sign points toward Silver Star Mountain.

Drop down the embankment roughly 150 to 200 ft to Early Winters Creek and cross on a log. Logjams shift year to year, so scout up and down for the best crossing and be prepared to ford in high water or early season when the creek runs cold and fast with snowmelt. Treat this crossing as your LAST RELIABLE WATER until camp.

On the far bank pick up the unofficial but well-defined climbers' trail that climbs the timbered rib on the WEST (left) side of the Burgundy Creek drainage. From there it climbs relentlessly and steeply through forest and brush for roughly 2,500-3,000 ft with almost no switchbacks and only fleeting water access early on. The tread erodes and is easy to lose in the timber.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The unmistakable break on this approach is THE BENCH, at roughly 6,400-6,700 ft: the grade suddenly eases onto an open larch-and-heather shelf with several established campsites and usually a seasonal trickle or snowmelt nearby. That is the standard overnight camp and the natural turnaround check for a day trip.

Above the bench there is a gully running obviously and directly to Burgundy Col. THAT GULLY IS THE WRONG ONE — it is loose and exposed. Instead stay LEFT and follow the trail up the gully directly above camp. Within it, stay climber's LEFT of the gully proper: the bed holds loose microwave-sized blocks, while the left side is unpleasant kitty-litter-covered slab but far less dangerous. Near the head of the gully make an ascending traverse to the RIGHT, under the cliffs, over heather-covered slabs into the col at roughly 7,800 ft. This gully and traverse is where parties describe the real crux of route-finding, both up and down. The col — not the glacier — is where the route proper begins; from there trend toward the northeast side of the west summit.
hazards: Early Winters Creek crossing — log can be wet, mossy or washed out; ford in high water
Steep eroding brushy tread that is easy to lose in the timber
Loose microwave-sized blocks in the gully bed above the bench
Loose kitty-litter slabs on the final traverse into the col
No water between the creek and the bench

approach_variants.name: Colchuck Lake outlet, east-side talus to the col
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
approach_variants.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead (FS Road 7601 off Icicle Creek Road). Colchuck Lake Trail #1599 runs 4 miles and 2,280 ft to the lake outlet in about two and a half to three hours; the lake is the last reliable water.

At the lake take the LEFT fork and stay high on the ridge, avoiding the spur trails that drop to the water's edge. Continue to the small dam near the lake's north end and cross the outlet creek at or just below it. Pick up the trail on the far side and follow it south roughly 100 yards to a slight clearing with boulders and talus on the LEFT.
approach_variants.baseFinding: The clearing with boulders and talus on the left, about 100 yards south of the outlet crossing, is the turn — it is easy to walk past. Ascend the talus angling slightly left into the woods and negotiate a brief 3rd/4th class rock step, using roots and branches as holds; that step is the confirmation you are on the right line and not on a lakeside spur. From there the path climbs southward through open, cairned forest for about an hour to the col, which overlooks a boulder-strewn camp area with views of Dragontail and Colchuck peaks.
hazards: Outlet creek crossing at the dam
Brief 3rd/4th class rock step gained on vegetation
Loose talus
No water above the lake

approach_variants.name: Colchuck Lake outlet into the west cirque
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
approach_variants.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead (NF-7601 off Icicle Creek Road; Northwest Forest Pass). Trail #1599 for about 2.25 miles, crossing Mountaineer Creek on a log bridge near the 1.5-mile mark, to the signed junction where Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A splits left. Cross Mountaineer Creek a second time on a log bridge, then climb steepening rocky switchbacks to Colchuck Lake — about 4 miles and 2,280 ft, roughly one and three-quarter to three hours depending on load.

Colchuck Lake is the LAST RELIABLE WATER; the basin and the wall are dry, though a spring at the base of the boulder field below the formation has been reported and should not be relied on.

The shorter of the two ways into the west basin: from the lake's north end, cross the outlet BELOW the small dam and follow a climbers' path up and across the timbered hillside directly into the cirque below the wall — about an hour from the lake, plus 15 to 25 minutes of boulder-hopping to reach the actual base.
approach_variants.baseFinding: Let It Burn starts in the base gully on the wall's lower-LEFT section, and the last move of the approach is a scramble up a THIRD-CLASS RAMP out of the gully to the foot of the technical climbing. Ramp, not gully floor — belaying from the gully bed means you are below the start. A documented party took about three hours and 47 minutes from trailhead to base, which matches the three-and-a-half to four hour figure the route carries; substantially longer usually means the alder band or the wrong gully.
hazards: Mountaineer Creek log bridges slick or partly submerged in high early-season flow
Loose 3rd/4th class rock in the final scramble to the wall
Loose basin talus
Long dry stretch above the lake

approach_variants.name: Aasgard-side lakeshore, slide alder, leftmost gully
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep; ice axe useful before mid-July
approach_variants.notes:
The longer southern option, which avoids the outlet crossing. From Colchuck Lake follow the lakeshore climbers' path counter-clockwise toward the slopes below Aasgard Pass, gaining talus and heather to roughly 400 ft above the lake in 30 to 40 minutes. That slope holds wet snow into July and has a real slip-and-fall history.

Cut north / climber's-LEFT off the Aasgard trail through a band of dense slide alder and heather — genuinely a bushwhack, 15 to 20 minutes, with a cairned path through it if you can find it. Once past the alder, take the LEFT-MOST gully and climb it about 1,000 ft to its top, then contour east on an easy path into the west basin. One and a half to two hours from the lake.
approach_variants.baseFinding: There are a couple of cairns at the BASE of the correct gully and none above it, so do not expect to be led up. Leftmost is the discriminator: a gully further right will not top out into the basin. From the basin, Let It Burn starts on the wall's lower-left section, and the technical climbing begins above a third-class ramp out of the base gully rather than at the gully floor.
hazards: Wet snow on the Aasgard slope into July
Dense slide alder band — a real bushwhack
Loose gully talus; snow lingering in the gully into early summer
Cairns stop at the base of the gully

approach_variants.name: Colchuck Lake outlet into the west cirque
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
approach_variants.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead (NF-7601 off Icicle Creek Road; Northwest Forest Pass). Stuart Lake Trail #1599 for roughly 2.25 miles with a Mountaineer Creek log bridge near 1.5 miles, to the junction where Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A branches left; a second Mountaineer Creek log crossing, then steepening rocky switchbacks to Colchuck Lake — about 4 miles and 2,280 ft, roughly one and three-quarter to two hours for a fit party.

The shorter line into the west basin: cross the lake's outlet below the small dam at the north end and follow the climbers' path up and across the timbered hillside straight into the cirque — about an hour from the lake, plus 15 to 25 minutes of boulder-hopping to the wall. Colchuck Lake is the last dependable water; carry what you need for a long day.
approach_variants.baseFinding: In the basin, The Scoop starts to the RIGHT of the West Face and the Tempest and to the LEFT of Rikki Tikki Tavi. The confirmation is not at the ground but three pitches up: the first three pitches, to about 5.10a, lead to LAUNCH LEDGE, the platform sitting directly below the namesake Scoop corner. If the ledge you reach after three pitches has no large corner system rising above it, you are not on The Scoop. Expect loose 3rd/4th class rock in the final approach scramble to the wall.
hazards: Slick or partly submerged log bridges over Mountaineer Creek early season
Loose talus in the basin and the final scramble
No water above Colchuck Lake
Snow lingering in the basin into early summer

approach_variants.name: Aasgard-side lakeshore, slide alder, leftmost gully
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep; ice axe useful before mid-July
approach_variants.notes: Follow the lakeshore climbers' path counter-clockwise toward the Aasgard Pass slopes, gaining talus and heather about 400 ft above the lake, then cut north through the slide-alder band — cairned, but a genuine bushwhack of 15 to 20 minutes. Take the LEFT-MOST gully and climb it about 1,000 ft to its top, then contour east on an easy path into the basin. One and a half to two hours from the lake, more gain than the outlet line but no ford.
approach_variants.baseFinding: Cairns mark the base of the correct gully and stop there. Leftmost is the test. From the basin, The Scoop is right of the West Face and Tempest and left of Rikki Tikki Tavi; Launch Ledge, three pitches up with the Scoop corner above it, is what confirms the line.
hazards: Wet snow on the Aasgard slope into July
Dense slide alder
Loose gully talus; late snow in the gully

approach_variants.name: Aasgard-side lakeshore, slide alder, base gully
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
approach_variants.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead (FS Road 7601 off Icicle Creek Road, about 8.5 miles from Leavenworth). Colchuck Lake Trail #1599: the first 1.5 miles climb gently through forest along Mountaineer Creek to a log-bridge crossing; about a mile past that, stay RIGHT at the signed junction with the Lake Stuart Trail. The final push switchbacks up a boulder moraine to the Colchuck Lake outlet — about 4 miles and 2,280 ft, two and a half to three hours at a steady pace. Fill water here; it is the last reliable source.

Work around toward the lake's south/east side and pick up the cairned Aasgard Pass climbers' trail, following it up steep talus and heather to roughly 400 ft above the lake in 30 to 40 minutes. That slope holds snow into July and has a real slip-and-fall history. Break off climber's-LEFT through the band of dense slide alder and heather — the brushy crux of the walk in, 15 to 20 minutes — to the base of the gully system below the main wall.
approach_variants.baseFinding: The Tempest begins at the CENTRE of the face, below the long bulge and roof, roughly mid-way along the base of the wall — a little RIGHT of where the West Face starts out of the gully. The overhanging bulge above is the feature to sight on: if there is no roof over your head, you are either left at the West Face's gully start or right toward The Scoop. Expect loose 3rd/4th class rock in the final approach scramble; many parties rope up for it. Three and a half to four hours trailhead to base.
hazards: Slick log bridges over Mountaineer Creek in high early-season flow
Wet snow on the Aasgard slope into July
Dense slide alder band
Loose 3rd/4th class ground in the final scramble to the wall

approach_variants.name: Colchuck Lake east shore to the Jabberwocky Tower notch
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
approach_variants.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead (FS Road 7601 off Icicle Creek Road). Colchuck Lake Trail #1599 for 4 miles and 2,280 ft — Mountaineer Creek log bridge at 1.5 miles, stay RIGHT at the Lake Stuart Trail junction — to Colchuck Lake in about two and a half to three hours. Last water.

This route is NOT approached through the west basin. Work around the EASTERN shoreline and talus instead. One documented ascent recorded roughly 4,760 ft of total gain and a twelve-hour car-to-car day.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The marker is a piece of rock, not a path: JABBERWOCKY TOWER, the granite spire standing between Colchuck Lake and Colchuck Balanced Rock. From the east shore, find the obvious gully that splits toward the NOTCH ABOVE that spire and ascend it — loose in places, with rope-up terrain in its upper section — to the notch. From the notch you step onto class 3 ground on the NW Ridge proper, and the climbing starts there.

Negative marker: the cairned climbers' path that leads left off the Aasgard trail through slide alder into the west basin goes to the West Face, The Scoop and the rest of the wall routes, and it leads AWAY from this one. If you are bushwhacking through alder you are on the west-side approach and on the wrong side of the formation.
hazards: Loose rock in the gully below the notch
Rope-up terrain in the upper gully
No water above Colchuck Lake
Long day — twelve hours car to car is documented
